match.reason: The bank has no point that links transform boundaries to stress build-up and earthquakes: the earthquake point covers all plate boundaries and volcanoes, while the boundary point covers transform motion without explaining earthquakes, so a new point is needed.

draft.title: Transform boundaries and earthquakes
card: At a transform boundary, two plates slide past each other sideways. Crust is not made or destroyed here.
The plate edges are rough and can lock together. The plates keep trying to move, so stress builds up in the rock.
When the stress becomes too great, the rock slips suddenly. The stored energy is released as shaking, which is an earthquake.
The San Andreas Fault in California is a transform boundary. The Pacific Plate and North American Plate slide past each other there.
draft.remember: Plates sliding past each other lock, build up stress, then slip suddenly as an earthquake.

a.q: Why do earthquakes happen along a transform boundary?
opts: Stress builds up as plates lock, then is released suddenly
Magma rises and pushes the plates apart slowly
One plate sinks and melts into the mantle
The plates crumple smoothly into mountain ranges
a.why: Plates sliding past each other can lock together while stress builds. When the rock slips, the stored energy is released as an earthquake. Magma rising to make new crust is not what happens at a transform boundary.
a.clue: Think about plates catching on each other as they slide.

b.q: Two plates are sliding past each other along a fault in the town of Karrin. Nothing has moved for many years, but the plates are still pushing. What is most likely to be happening to the rock along the fault?
opts: Stress is building up and may be released suddenly
New crust is forming along the fault
The plates have stopped moving, so no earthquake can occur
Crust is being destroyed beneath one plate
b.why: The plates keep pushing even when the edges are locked, so stress builds up. It may later be released as an earthquake. Calm years do not mean the plates have stopped moving.
b.clue: The plates keep moving even if the edges are stuck.

problems.detail: The stem says 'Nothing has moved for many years', but the clue and why say the plates keep moving and only the locked edges are stuck. A student may read the stem as the plates having stopped, which is the idea a distractor tests. Saying 'The fault has not slipped for many years' would remove the clash.
